{{Short description|German–Jewish chemist who settled in Britain (1925–2013)}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=April 2022}}
'''Peter Ludwig Israel Pauson''' [[FRSE]] [[FRIC]] (1925–2013) was a German–Jewish emigrant who settled in Britain and who is remembered for his contributions to chemistry, most notably the [[Pauson–Khand reaction]]<ref name="SciencedirectS0040402001914243">{{cite journal|title=The khand reaction : A convenient and general route to a wide range of cyclopentenone derivatives|journal=Tetrahedron|author=Peter L. Pauson|volume=41|issue=24|year=1985|pages=5855–5860|doi=10.1016/S0040-4020(01)91424-3}}</ref> and as joint discoverer of [[ferrocene]].<ref name="researchgate">{{cite web|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/260950792|title=Peter Ludwig Pauson (1925-2013) {{pipe}} Request PDF|website=researchgate.net|access-date=27 August 2018}}</ref>

==Life==

He was born in [[Bamberg]], [[Germany]] on 30 July 1925, the son of Stefan Pauson and his wife, Helene Dorothea Herzfelder.<ref name="geni">{{cite web|url=https://www.geni.com/people/Peter-Pauson/6000000031489017285|title=Peter Ludwig Pauson (1925 - 2013) - Genealogy|website=geni.com|access-date=27 August 2018}}</ref> His parents escaped to England in 1939 with Peter and his two sisters to flee the Nazi persecution of Jews.<ref name="juden-in-bamberg">{{cite web|url=http://www.juden-in-bamberg.de/Letter_from_bamberg/Letter_16/28_lfb.htm|website=juden-in-bamberg.de|title=Juden in Bamberg|access-date=27 August 2018}}</ref>{{dead link|date=July 2026}}

In 1942 the family moved to [[Glasgow]] and he began studying chemistry in the [[University of Glasgow]] under [[Thomas Stevens Stevens]]. After graduating in 1946, he moved to [[Sheffield University]] as a postgraduate, studying under [[Robert Downs Haworth]] and receiving his doctorate in 1949. He then went to [[Duquesne University]] in [[Pittsburgh]], Pennsylvania and pursued research on [[tropolone]]s and other aromatic non-benzenoid molecules. His discovery of [[ferrocene]] with his student, [[Thomas J. Kealy]], arose from an attempt to dimerize [[cyclopentadienylmagnesium bromide]] using [[Iron(III) chloride]]; the orange-yellow solid with formula C<sub>10</sub>H<sub>10</sub>Fe was described as a "molecular sandwich" in Pauson's note which was published in ''Nature'' in 1951.<ref name="Chemistryworld7617"/>

From 1951 to 1952 he studied at the [[University of Chicago]] under [[Morris Kharasch]], then becoming a [[DuPont]] Fellow at [[Harvard University]]. He then gained practical experience at the DuPont Laboratories in [[Wilmington, Delaware|Wilmington]]. Returning to Britain, he became a lecturer at Sheffield University and in 1959 became Professor of Organic Chemistry at [[Strathclyde University]]. In 1964 he was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society of Edinburgh]].<ref>{{cite book|title=Biographical Index of Former Fellows of the Royal Society of Edinburgh 1783–2002|date=July 2006|publisher=The Royal Society of Edinburgh|isbn=0-902-198-84-X|url=https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|access-date=27 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304074135/https://www.royalsoced.org.uk/cms/files/fellows/biographical_index/fells_indexp2.pdf|archive-date=4 March 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Pauson and his postdoctoral assistant, Ihsan Khand, discovered the reaction now renowned as the [[Pauson–Khand reaction]] in 1971, though Pauson always referred to it as the "Khand reaction".<ref name="Chemistryworld7617"/>

In 1994, the University of Strathclyde established the [[Merck Group|Merck]] Pauson Chair in Preparative Chemistry, funded by Merck, marking the contribution of Pauson to chemistry and to the university.<ref name="Times1994Mar21">{{cite newspaper The Times|url=http://find.galegroup.com/ttda/infomark.do?&source=gale&prodId=TTDA&userGroupName=hamlib&tabID=T003&docPage=article&searchType=BasicSearchForm&docId=IF502026301&type=multipage&contentSet=LTO&version=1.0|title=University of Strathclyde|department=Display Advertising|date=21 March 1994|page=36|issue=64907|access-date=28 August 2018}}</ref>

Pauson retired in 1995 and died peacefully at home on 10 December 2013. He was cremated at [[Clydebank]] Crematorium.<ref name="legacy">{{cite web|url=https://www.legacy.com/obituaries/name/peter-pauson-obituary?pid=168598346|title=Peter PAUSON Obituary|website=Legacy.com|date=16 December 2013 |access-date=27 August 2018}}</ref> In his obituary, he is described as "''a gentleman of modesty, humility, and compassion … a fine man and a marvellous scientist''".<ref name="Chemistryworld7617"/>

==Family==

He married Lai-Ngau Mary (née Wong) (1928 – March 18, 2010),<ref name="Geni6000000030908748493">{{cite web|url=https://www.geni.com/people/Lai-Ngau-Pauson/6000000030908748493|title=Lai-Ngau Mary Pauson (Wong) (1928 - 2010) - Genealogy|website=geni.com|date=26 March 2017 |access-date=2 September 2018}}</ref> having met her at a party hosted by [[Enrico Fermi]] when Pauson was at the University of Chicago in the early 1950s.<ref name="Chemistryworld7617">{{cite web|url=https://www.chemistryworld.com/opinion/april-2014/7617.article|title=Peter Pauson (1925–2013)|author=William Kerr|year=2014|website=Chemistry World|access-date=2 September 2018}}</ref> They went on to have two children, Hilary and Alfred.<ref name="Legacy-Ia3769391">{{cite web|url=https://legacy-ia.com/obituary/pauson-lai-ngau-mary/3769391?s_source=nqgl_her|title=Pauson - Lai-Ngau (Mary) : Obituary : Herald|website=legacy-ia.com|access-date=2 September 2018}}</ref>{{dead link|date=July 2026}}
